author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: My father's family name being Pirrip, and my Christian name Philip, my infant tongue could make of both names nothing longer or more explicit than Pip. So, I called myself Pip, and came to be called Pip by the universe at large, embracing the profound simplicity of that single syllable.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: I give Pirrip as my father's family name, on the authority of his tombstone and my sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, who married the blacksmith. As I never saw my father or my mother, and never saw any likeness of either of them—for their days were long before the days of photographs—my first fancies regarding what they were like were unreasonably derived from the cold stone that marked their final resting place.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: The shape of the letters on my father's grave gave me an odd idea that he was a square, stout, dark man, with curly black hair. From the character and turn of the inscription, 'Also Georgiana Wife of the Above,' I drew a childish, yet deeply held conclusion that my mother was freckled and sickly, forever destined to rest 'below' the stout and square Pirrip.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: To five little stone lozenges, each about a foot and a half long, which were arranged in a neat row beside their grave, and were sacred to the memory of five little brothers of mine, who gave up trying to get a living exceedingly early in that universal struggle, I am indebted for a belief I religiously entertained that they had all been born on their backs with their hands in their trousers-pockets, and had never taken them out in this state of existence.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: Ours was the marsh country, down by the river, within, as the river wound, twenty miles of the sea. My sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, who was more than twenty years older than I, had established a great reputation with herself and the neighbours because she had brought me up 'by hand,' a phrase that carried with it a terrifying implication of physical discipline.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: My first most vivid and broad impression of the identity of things, seems to me to have been gained on a memorable raw afternoon towards evening. At such a time I found out for certain, that this bleak place overgrown with nettles was the churchyard, and that Philip Pirrip, late of this parish, and also Georgiana wife of the above, were dead and buried.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: The dark flat wilderness beyond the churchyard, intersected with dykes and mounds and gates, with scattered cattle feeding on it, was the marshes; and that the low leaden line beyond was the river; and that the dark flat wilderness beyond that again was the sea; and that the small bundle of shivers growing afraid of it all and beginning to cry, was Pip.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: “Hold your noise!” cried a terrible voice, as a man started up from among the graves at the side of the church porch. “Keep still, you little devil, or I’ll cut your throat!” The voice was so sudden and terrifying that it stopped my tears instantly, freezing the blood in my young veins.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: A fearful man, all in coarse grey, with a great iron on his leg. A man with no hat, and with broken shoes, and with an old rag tied round his head. A man who had been soaked in water, and smothered in mud, and lamed by stones, and cut by flints, and stung by nettles, and torn by briars; who limped, and shivered, and glared and growled.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: He limped, and shivered, and glared and growled; and his teeth chattered in his head as he seized me by the chin. “O! Don’t cut my throat, sir,” I pleaded in terror. “Pray don’t do it, sir.” I clung to the cold stone of a tomb, praying that this terrifying apparition would spare my miserable life.
